description: The puzzle build demo: which puzzle, where the base goes, how each piece is gripped. Positions are in the cell's world frame: metres, z = 0 on the bench top, the rail along x, the table toward -y. Grasps are in each piece's own CAD frame.

survey.what: Wrist D415 straight down, gripper closed. The camera always sees its own gripper: it fills the top middle of the picture and the fingertips end at the picture's centre, so the point looked at is on the robot's side of the base in the middle and to its left, and nothing of the base is hidden.
survey.why_there: The pose has to be one the real cell allows. Over [0.02, -0.37] at 0.72 m, where this survey used to stand, wrist 3 is at 141.5 degrees and the camera's cord needs 13.2 cm more than at the real scan pose: the real cell's wrist 3 window ends at 135 degrees and its cord's spare loop is taken as 10 cm (the puzzle project's ros2/config; both guesses until measured). From 0.145 m further along -x wrist 3 is at 114 degrees and the cord needs 9.2 cm. From 0.75 m the picture reaches x = 0.40 and y = -0.66 at 0.81 mm a pixel (0.78 before), and the flange stays 14 mm under the 0.80 m top of the bridge's workspace box.

arm.what: Where wrist 3 is kept when a pose leaves the choice (which way round a piece is gripped, and whether it is turned on the table first): wrist_3_deg is the range for the pick and the place, and from the pick to the place it may turn up by no more than wrist_3_rise_deg. Both are read off the cord model of the puzzle project's GaP bridge (10 cm of spare loop, not measured) on this build's own moves: a pick above 100 degrees needs more cord than that, and so does a carry that turns wrist 3 up through more than about 100 degrees (a bar picked at -40 and put in at 69 needs 10.6 cm, one picked at -20 needs 3.8). Not a limit of the simulated arm: a grasp outside it is still taken when the piece is not turned, and the bridge then refuses it. turn_on_table: whether a piece no way of holding keeps there is turned where it lies before it is picked (turn_grasps). Off: in the builds measured so far a turned bar and one turned fork were seated, and another fork, turned, jammed in its slot in four builds of four where the same fork picked as it lay was seated in three of three. The fingers hold a fork by the top of its tab and it slides in them by 0 to 7.5 mm from one pick to the next; until they hold it repeatably a turn trades seats for goals the bridge sends.

scan.what: The scan step's views after the survey's own (straight down, the view the matcher reads), taken only when the view from above leaves a piece in doubt: where the wrist camera is, the point it looks at, and its turn about the line of sight. The depth of every view is compared with the matched pieces, which is what tells a piece's rival poses apart. Five frames a view, the number the matcher reads. Each view, and each move between them, was chosen inside the real cell's limits as the puzzle project's GaP bridge holds them (joint and cable windows, at most 10 cm of camera cord, the workspace box): the sweep top, left, right, top needs 9.2, 7.7 and 9.2 cm of cord. The left view sees every piece; the right one, rolled a sixth of a turn to stay inside those limits, sees the base and what lies to its right and lines up poorly (cost 0.14 against the left view's 0.002): it adds little, and no better one was found inside the limits.

base_check.what: The fast check of the base while a piece is brought to it (scripts/puzzle_base_check.py): one depth picture of the wrist camera at the pre-place hover and after every descent_step_m of lowering, fitted with the base's CAD from its last pose. The camera rides on the gripper and looks along it: a piece that goes in with the gripper level (the forks) is checked once instead, from look (offset_m from the base's middle, height_m above the table, roll_deg about the line of sight: a pose with wrist 3 at 16 degrees, where the base is wholly in the picture beside the gripper), before it is carried in, and not again. A base found more than moved_mm or moved_deg away, by a fit that is trusted, takes its slots and seated pieces with it and the rest of the placement is laid out again (and simulated ahead when the build simulates ahead); at most corrections times per placement. moved_mm was 3.0: a look keeps a filled base's last pose unless it finds it 3 mm away, so the base could lie that far from where the robot had it, and a fork put in 2.6 mm off jammed (seed 3). Over 124 kept checks the trusted fit was 0.26 mm from the truth (median; 1.1 mm at the 95th percentile), and in all 18 that read 1.5 to 3 mm it was nearer the truth than the pose it was compared with. A fit that is not trusted, or other pieces not where they were, puts the piece back and scans the table.

base_target.what: The middle of the table. The yaw puts the forks' slots across the rail, so each fork is brought in from its own side with the gripper level; the base may also arrive half a turn round.

grip_force_source: The lab's RG2 driver (RISL_onrobot_ros, custom_libraries/onrobot.py) sends force_val=400, in units of 0.1 N, with every move: 40 N, the RG2's maximum (datasheet: 3 to 40 N). Not measured on the real gripper.

turn_grasps.what: How a piece is gripped to be turned on the table when no way of holding it keeps wrist 3 where arm says. A fork is held one way round, and that grip half a turn round is no help (when the one is outside the range the other is inside, and a turn that brings the first inside takes the second out): it is turned by a grip a quarter turn from its own, along its middle, across the 69.9 mm from the end of the centre tab to the tip of the centre prong. A bar is turned by its own grip.

fork_orange.what: Along the middle, tab end to centre prong tip.

base3.what: The centre island between the two bar slots, across its 23.1 mm width; the fingertips stand in the bar slots. The island is 7 mm high, enough to slide the plate on the table and not to lift it.

line_brown.what: Across the bar's 25.9 mm width at its middle, the pads' lower edge 7.5 mm above the face the bar lies on: with the bar on the slot floor that is 0.5 mm above the 7 mm slot walls.

fork_orange.what: The centre tab across its 21 mm width, from the fork's flat side: the fork is picked lying flat and turned upright in the hand, and goes into its slot with the gripper level.

corrected_from_table.what: The pieces whose place --correction table shifts by the table's entry for their type (scripts/puzzle_build_corrections.json); a measuring run (--write-corrections) rehearses exactly these. The forks: picked lying flat by the tab and turned upright in the hand, they sit 1.5 to 6.5 mm from the grasp as defined. Not the bars: a bar sits 0.4 to 3.4 mm off in no steady direction, a correction lowers the gripper (the arm hangs about 1 mm low at the pick, so the pads hold the bar lower than defined), and the bar's grasp leaves the pads only 0.5 mm above the slot's walls. With the bars corrected too the build seated 18 of 24 pieces over six layouts, against 23 of 24 without (2026-11-17).

table_camera.what: A second camera for the video only: any camera on a tripod beyond the table's far edge. Off unless --table-camera is given; drawn on the stage for the run, not part of the ur5e-workcell pack, and no step of the build reads it.
